newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ten indicted over collapse of South Korea's Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: Ten indicted over collapse of South Korea's Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors on Wednesday indicted 10 people over the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in a loans-for-kickback scandal that has rocked the government of President Kim Young-sam.
Nine of those indicted, including three close aides to Kim, are already in detention in connection with the scandal. The 10th is in jail over an unrelated case.
Prosecutors said their probe into what is probably the biggest corporate collapse in South Korean history was at the half-way stage.

Choi Byung-koog, a senior prosecutor, told reporters the investigation had run into problems because key evidence had been destroyed, including Hanbo's account books before 1993. Cash bribes were hard to track down.
The prosecution was depending heavily on testimony by Hanbo Group founder Chung Tai-soo, one of those detained along with former company treasurer Kim Jong-kook.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of the Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th biggest conglomerate, was declared insolvent on January 23 after racking up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans.
"So far we've had a hard time finding truth behind the case that would clear up all suspicions," Choi said.
"We had to rely mostly on Chung's testimony, and he has insisted he didn't have to bribe many government officials because bankers and politicians did the job."
Choi said the prosecution was still trying to account for 25 billion won in loans.
"We'll continue to track down where the funds have gone and find out whether Chung's family has hidden assets," he said.
Those indicted in Kim Young-sam's inner circle include former home affairs minister Kim Woo-suk, who resigned last Wednesday before being held on charges of accepting bribes.
The other two presidential confidants are lawmakers Hong In-gil and Hwang Byung-tai, key members of a faction that backed Kim Young-sam's rise to power.
Another member of parliament, Chung Jae-chull, the highest-ranking official in the ruling New Korea Party after the president and party chairman, was also indicted.

Three bankers have been indicted, including two former presidents of Korea First Bank, Hanbo's major creditor. One former president, Rhee Chul-soo, is serving a three-year jail sentence after being convicted of bribery in a separate case. The other is Sheen Kwang-shik.
The third banker is Woo Chan-mok, head of Cho Hung Bank.
Chung was arrested on charges of fraud and violating laws on issuing cheques and trust and savings companies.
Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, was also indicted.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics blasted the report.

"It looks like the prosecution has spent 20 days working on ways to hide the truth and deceive the public," a party statement said. "The investigation failed to uncover who is really behind all those loans."
The National Congress has accused President Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, of playing a key role in brokering loans to Hanbo.
Kim Hyun-chul has filed criminal complaints against politicians who made such allegations, and is due to be summoned by prosecutors looking into his complaints.
